chunks: "On an eye diagram the two impairments show up in different directions.
Timing jitter is the horizontal blur: the crossing points, where rising and falling edges intersect, spread out sideways instead of landing at one point, and that cuts the eye width.
Amplitude noise is the vertical blur: the high and low levels aren't thin lines, they have thickness, and that cuts the eye height. To quantify them you take histograms.
A horizontal histogram of where the edges cross the mid-level gives the jitter distribution, and its standard deviation or peak-to-peak is the jitter.
A vertical histogram at the centre of the eye gives the distribution of the 1 and 0 levels, whose width is the noise, and the separation of the two humps over their widths gives the Q factor.
You can tell the types apart by shape. Random jitter or noise gives smooth Gaussian tails that fade out.

Deterministic effects have bounded, often distinct bands: ISI gives several discrete crossing positions or level bands, duty-cycle distortion shifts rising and falling crossings apart, and periodic jitter gives a two-lobed histogram.
They're also linked: amplitude noise on a sloped edge becomes timing jitter, so the crossing blur has a contribution from noise, divided by the slew rate."
